SOURCE EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING ITS METHOD
SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the Scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” that the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, Scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very Scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the Scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/29-sun-moon-and-stars.adoc

This book is about the symbolic language of the Bible, and little is more symbolic than the speech the sky pours forth, day after day and night after night — knowledge shown without a word, in every tongue at once.
All creation testifies, and Scripture provides the key that unlocks the symbolic meaning of the sun, the moon, and the stars; with their meaning unlocked, we can come to understand how they govern the day and the night.

The method is the one this book has used from its first chapter: search the Scriptures for every reference to the sun, the moon, and the stars, decode their symbolic meaning, and watch that meaning reflected in the very structure of creation.
And the stakes are not academic: “He appointed the moon for seasons” (Psalm 104:19) — the appointed times — and the announcement of the gospel itself carries the command to keep them:

Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace!
O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows…

The bringer of the good tidings and the command to keep the feasts arrive in one breath; and it will take wisdom to discern the truth of the matter.

From the first page of Scripture the lights of heaven are given a job, and it is not merely to glow.
The founding verse [Footnote: The King James closes the verse “he made the stars also” — but the Hebrew has no second “made” and no “also”; the sentence runs straight on from the lesser light's commission to the stars, as rendered here.], in its own order:

And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night with the stars.

The Psalm that recounts the same creation leaves no doubt:

The sun to rule by day… The moon and stars to rule by night: for his mercy endureth for ever.

The stars are no afterthought scattered in the dark; they rule the night together with the moon — “the ordinances of the moon and of the stars for a light by night” (Jeremiah 31:35).
The greater light governs the day; the lesser light and the stars govern the night.

The Hebrew names the two lights with the family's own words.
“Greater” and “lesser” are ha-gadol and ha-qaton — the very pair the King James itself renders “her eldest son Esau… her younger son Jacob” (Genesis 27:15), and “the name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel” (Genesis 29:16).
Read the founding verse with the family's own vocabulary, and it says what Joseph will dream: the elder light to rule the day, and the younger light to rule the night with the stars — a household hung in the sky from the fourth day.

Scripture keeps a portrait of the younger.
When Samuel asks Jesse for his sons, “There remaineth yet the youngest” — ha-qaton — “and, behold, he keepeth the sheep” (1 Samuel 16:11); and David the qaton, the anointed shepherd, is the name the prophets give the Messiah centuries after David slept:

And I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd.

Two offices are written into the lights at the founding: they are set “to rule” (Genesis 1:16-18), and to be “for signs, and for seasons” (Genesis 1:14) — to mark the appointed times.

Scripture interprets its own symbol.
Joseph dreams of the heavens bowing, and his father reads the dream on the spot:

…behold, the sun and the moon and the eleven stars made obeisance to me… Shall I and thy mother and thy brethren indeed come to bow down ourselves to thee…?

Jacob does not hesitate: the sun is the father, the moon the mother, the eleven stars the brothers — Jacob, his wife, and the twelve sons who become the tribes.
The lights are read as persons: a governing household.
Lift the dream from the one family to the whole, and each light tells what it is.

The sun is the greatest light; the moon and the wandering stars shine only with what they borrow from it — so it stands for the source.
The dream named the sun the father, and the Psalm names Him outright:

For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory…

He alone shines of Himself; all other light is His light, handed on.

The verse holds a second office beside the first — a sun and shield — and the psalm has already said who the shield is, two verses up:

Behold, O God our shield, and look upon the face of thine anointed.

The shield is the Anointed — the one who stands between the source and the man.
Abram heard the office in the first person: “Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield” (Genesis 15:1).
And Moses felt it on the mountain: God's own hand held over him in the cleft while the glory passed by (Exodus 33:22). [Footnote: The Shadow chapter watched that hand cover Moses — the shadow of God's hand set between a man and His glory.]
The sun, and beside it the shield: the source, and the curved covering that hands on what a man can bear of it.

When the New Testament names Him by this office, it names the whole household with Him:

Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.

The “lights” He is Father of are the lights of this chapter — the lesser light and the stars, the children who shine with what He gives.

The verse sets the perfection not on the Father alone, but on what stands with Him — the Greek is par’ hō, beside whom.
The Hebrew text of James reads it the same way: every good gift comes down “from the light of the Father” — the letters under “from the light” spell ma'or, the luminary of the fourth day — and “beside him” (etslo, the close-company word) “there is no exchange of light and darkness.”

The light that stands beside the Father of lights with no variableness, neither shadow of turning is the Son — and of the moon's faces, exactly one carries no shadow of turning at all: the full, constant and complete the whole night it reigns.
And the Son of man has a face in the sky, by the Lord's own word:

And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.

A sign that appears in heaven — the fourth day's own vocabulary again, a sign of the lights — and the reader of this chapter now knows which face it is: the full, unshadowed witness.

Scripture has already named the good gift the Father of lights sends down from above.
On the fourth day, God “set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth” (Genesis 1:17).
The word translated set can also be translated gave, but give light already makes the point: the lights are a gift from above.
They were appointed “for signs, and for seasons”, the moedim, the appointed times, and “God saw that it was good” (Genesis 1:14-18).
Light from above, appointed for the appointed times, and pronounced good: the fourth day is James’ sentence, written forward.
And Moses says the giving reaches every people: the sun, the moon, and the stars, “which the LORD thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven” (Deuteronomy 4:19) — chalaq, to apportion, as lots are dealt — the appointed times are the portion the Father of lights deals to all under heaven.

That mark matters: a perfect and complete gift bears no shadow of turning — it will divide the true sign from the counterfeit when the counterfeit appears.

The moon rules the night, yet it has no light of its own — all it gives is the sun's light turned back to the earth.
That is the Son exactly: “The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do” (John 5:19); “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12) — light reflected, not self-made, the Father's light carried faithfully into the dark.
It is David's covenant psalm that seats his throne among the lights:

His seed shall endure for ever, and his throne as the sun before me.
It shall be established for ever as the moon, and as a faithful witness in heaven.

The Hebrew under “throne” is kisse — the same three letters as keseh, the full moon, an identity the Pearls of Wisdom chapter weighs verse by verse — and the word under “before me” is neged: in front of, facing — Strong's, “a part opposite; a counterpart, or mate” — the very word of the helper made “meet for him” (Genesis 2:18).

His throne as the sun facing me: exactly one light stands opposite the sun and returns his whole face, and so the psalm's next breath names the seat for what it is — the throne, the full moon, established forever, the faithful witness in the sky.

The word testifies that the throne stands to the sun as the wife stands to her husband — the ezer ke-negdo, the helper who is his counterpart and mate.
Joseph's dream read the moon as the wife and mother; the psalm has already seated her as the sun's neged — two witnesses, and at the mouth of two witnesses the matter is established: the moon is the sun's symbolic wife, the counterpart who stands facing him.

The stones that picture this throne — one pearl, and the sapphire pavement under His feet — wait in the Pearls of Wisdom chapter, where the gem-symbols carry what the lights declare.

Revelation opens by handing the psalm's title to its Owner: “Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead” (Revelation 1:5) — the Faithful Witness is the Messiah's own name, and the moon is that name written in the sky.
Genesis called the moon ha-qaton, the lesser light; Samuel called David ha-qaton, the youngest, out keeping the sheep.
The qaton son who kept the sheep holds the qaton light's throne.

The lesser light that governs the night is the Son, bearing the Father's light through it.

The night it shines in is this present age — “the night cometh, when no man can work” (John 9:4); “the night is far spent, the day is at hand” (Romans 13:12).
Into that dark the Son came as its light:

And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.

The Greek under “comprehended” is katalaben — to seize, to take hold of — and it carries two readings, both true.
The Hebrew text of John reads the taking-hold as power: the gloom “does not have power over it” — the darkness cannot overpower the light.
And read as the mind's taking hold — understanding — the measure is the one the Fool and the Wise chapter fixed: understanding is the commandments done (Psalm 111:10) [Footnote: Derived in the chapter The Fool and the Wise.] — to understand a light is to walk by it.
The world's night could not put out its light, and would not obey it: the witness shines full in the dark, and the dark does not keep what it shows.

“As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John 9:5) — for a light that shines in the dark is the light of the night.
As the moon carries the sun's light while the sun is down and unseen, so the Son carries the Father's into the world's night, “a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn” (2 Peter 1:19) — until the righteous shine as the sun.
And one light keeps the verse's exact hours: the full moon rises as the sun sets and does not set until the day dawns — sunset to sunrise, the whole watch of the dark — the timetable of the promise hung in the sky.

The two dominions have their peoples: the children of light and of the day — the households the Light and Darkness chapter divided (1 Thessalonians 5:5). [Footnote: Derived in the Light and Darkness chapter.]
The day's children are the covenant righteous; the night is where the nations sit — “Galilee of the Gentiles; the people which sat in darkness saw great light” (Matthew 4:15-16).
And that is why the night is given governors at all: the moon and the stars are set over the night, the Son and His righteous carrying His light to the people in the dark.

The moon does not rule the night alone — “the moon and stars to rule by night” (Psalm 136:9) — and the stars that rule beside Him are named:

And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.

The wise — those who heard and did — are the stars; “ye are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14).

Note how a star shines, for it is not the moon's way.
The moon gives back a light that strikes it from without; a star burns — each one a fire of its own, shining from within.
That too is exact.
His light is not bounced off the righteous; it is kindled in them — “God… hath shined in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 4:6), “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:27) — treasure carried “in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

This book has already handled the vessel and the fuel: the commandment is the lamp and the law is the light (Proverbs 6:23), and what burns in the lamp is oil — the pressed and tested fruit of the tree — “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works” (Matthew 5:16).
The saints shine as the stars shine: a received fire burning from within, fruit alight in the lamp of the commandment; and so they rule the night at His side, through the long night of this age, until the morning.

This co-reign is stated as plainly as Scripture can state it:

Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him a thousand years.

John saw the scene open with the bench being seated — “I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given unto them… and they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years” (Revelation 20:4).
The stars are not ornaments of the night; they reign in it, with the Light that burns in them.

The stars are counted, and they come to twelve.
Joseph saw eleven, and himself the twelfth — the sons who became the tribes of Israel.
John sees them gathered into a crown:

And there was seen a great sign in the heavens: a certain woman clothed in the sun, and the moon under her feet; and from her head begins the cycle, the first of the twelve stars.

The covenant nation wears the whole of heaven — clothed with the sun, the moon at her feet, the year's round beginning at her head.
And the verse announces itself in the fourth day's own vocabulary: a great sign in the heavens — the words of the two great lights set in the heavens “for signs, and for seasons” (Genesis 1:14-16); what John saw is one of the signs the lights were hung to give.

Every choice in that rendering is the Hebrew's own. [Footnote: The Hebrew Revelation — the Cochin manuscript tradition, Ele Ha-Sodot, c. 1700, which also carries the Gospels, James, and Jude — is the second witness this book consults for New Testament wording. A complete interlinear, and the evidence for the text's legitimacy as a witness, is presented at https://TimeTested.Bible[TimeTested.Bible].]
The sign is nes — not a mere signal but a standard, raised high for every eye, the ensign-word of the “root of Jesse” (Isaiah 11:10).
The crown is kether, the royal crown of Esther — a circle of authority, and the circle a cycle: rule that runs a round; her “head” is rosh, the word every beginning opens with.
And echad stands twice in the sentence — one, a certain, first, the word of “the first day” (Genesis 1:5) — once counting the woman, and once, with min, ranking her: first of the twelve.

The counted sign can be read in the sky itself.
The stars of God gather into constellations, the “Mazzaroth” He brings forth in their season (Job 38:32), and His people gather into the twelve tribes, the constellations of His heaven — and of the twelve figures of that circuit, exactly one is a woman: Virgo, the virgin.

A bride wears the sun by receiving and reflecting its light.
Not by the sun standing in her — a figure in which the sun stands rides the sky by day, washed invisible in his glare, a sign no eye could ever see — but by the full moon standing in her, delivering the whole of the sun's light from directly opposite: the Bridegroom clothing his bride — a relay this chapter is about to draw whole.

Her feet are answered too, for the moon under them is not a footstool of contempt; it is the stone she stands on.
Scripture names the believer's footing — “and that Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4); “upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18); “he… set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings” (Psalm 40:2) — the psalm this book's Introduction stood on.
The woman clothed by her Bridegroom stands on her Rock: the bride upon the moon, the assembly upon Christ.

Isaiah names the day when that picture is fulfilled:

Moreover the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, in the day that the LORD bindeth up the breach of his people, and healeth the stroke of their wound.

On that day the moon wears the sun's own brightness — the bride clothed to the full — and the sun blazes sevenfold.
It is a healing day, the breach bound up.
The lights do not trade places; the Husband raises His wife's light to His own.
From her the circuit begins — Virgo, the sign of Issachar, the tribe of “men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do” (1 Chronicles 12:32) — and the full moon standing at her feet marks the head of the year.

The lights, then, are read straight through: the Father the sun, the Son the moon that bears His light through the night, the righteous the stars that rule the night with Him, gathered into the twelve tribes.
And the promise to the stars is the sun's own brightness: “Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43).

Hold the offices together and a question surfaces that must be settled before the counterfeit: this chapter read the sun as the Father — yet Malachi calls the Son “the Sun of righteousness” (Malachi 4:2); it read the moon as the Son — yet Joseph's dream read her as the mother, and the Pearls of Wisdom chapter will price her as the pearl.
Do the symbols trade places?

They do not — they name offices, not persons: the source of light in a relation, and the faithful reflector in a relation.
And Scripture hangs the whole chain on one verse:

But I would have you know, that the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God.

Paul then restates the chain in light-language: the man is “the image and glory of God: but the woman is the glory of the man” (11:7), the very word he hangs on the sky — “one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon” (1 Corinthians 15:41).
Glory of is reflection-language: each bearer in the chain is moon to the one above, and sun to the one below.

.The relay of light — each bearer is moon to the one above, sun to the one below

Toward the Father the Son stands in the moon's office: “the brightness of his glory” (Hebrews 1:3), doing nothing of himself (John 5:19) — the faithful witness.
Toward the bride He stands in the sun's: the bridegroom of Psalm 19, “the Sun of righteousness” arising with the day.

The office keeps handing down the chain: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12) — “Ye are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14) — the same title, passed one link; and the Lord even time-stamped the transfer (John 9:5).
When the Sun left the sky, the moon and the stars carried His light through the night.

When one verse sets Jesus as sun and another sets Him as moon, neither has moved Him: the two texts stand on opposite sides of the same Man — one looking up the chain, one looking down.
And the world's long night will end the way the sky rehearses it every morning: the faithful witness of the night rises at the day as the Sun of righteousness, “with healing in his wings.”

If the stars are the righteous, the leaders of the righteous should stand among them by rank — and Scripture seats them there by name.
It calls the lights of the sky and the court around the throne by one name: Moses names “the sun, and the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven” (Deuteronomy 4:19); Micaiah sees the same host in session:

I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.

One phrase, both scenes: the stars are the host, and the host is the court.
Job heard them at the founding as a single choir — “the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (Job 38:7).

The court has a seated bench.
Daniel watched as “thrones were put in place” — plural — and “the court was seated” (Daniel 7:9-10, NKJV).
Jesus assigned twelve of the seats — “ye also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28); John saw the bench filled — “round about the throne… four and twenty elders sitting, clothed in white raiment” (Revelation 4:4).

Isaiah had already set that bench in the sky:

Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his elders, glory.

The moon, the sun, the LORD of hosts enthroned, and His elders in glory — one scene; and the old Greek translation renders the word presbyteroi, the very word of Revelation's twenty-four. [Footnote: The word is zaqen, the Bible's ordinary word for elders — the same word the King James renders “elders” throughout the law and the histories; here it prints “and before his ancients gloriously.”]

The seven stars of Revelation are “the messengers of the seven assemblies” (Revelation 1:20) — each assembly's leading light, held in the right hand.
The Hebrew Revelation makes the office explicit at both ends of the vision: it addresses the book “to the seven elders in Asia,” and reads the seven menorahs as “seven elders.”

Even the psalm of the faithful witness holds court and witness in one sky: the “congregation of the saints” meets where none “in the heaven” — the shachaq — “can be compared unto the LORD,” who is “to be had in reverence of all them that are about him” (Psalm 89:5-7); and thirty verses on, the moon stands “a faithful witness” in that same shachaq (89:37).
The elders of the assemblies stand among the host of heaven: the named and brightest of the stars.

What do the members of the court look like?
John describes animals, studded with eyes.

…and round about the throne, were four beasts full of eyes before and behind.
And the first beast was like a lion, and the second beast like a calf, and the third beast had a face as a man, and the fourth beast was like a flying eagle.

Ezekiel saw the same court with the same jewelling — rings “full of eyes round about” (Ezekiel 1:18) — and Scripture says plainly what such eyes are: “the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth” (Zechariah 4:10); “seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent forth into all the earth” (Revelation 5:6).
Eyes that travel the whole earth; watchers that are sent — the stars’ own commission, told in the stars’ own numbers.

Jesus says what an eye is in this language:

The lamp of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.

The word is lychnos, the lamp — built, Strong's notes, on leukos, white — and the lamp is where the wise keep their oil: “the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps” (Matthew 25:4).
Eyes that are burning lamps, and a court of figures full of them: the righteous alight, each body full of light, shining as the stars shine.

The Hebrew idiom tells what fills the lamp, or darkens it.
The “bountiful eye” is, in the letters, a good eye — tov ayin — and its goodness is giving: “he giveth of his bread to the poor” (Proverbs 22:9); the “evil eye” hoards its bread (Proverbs 23:6); and Jesus keeps the same pair in the lamp-saying itself — “but if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness” (Matthew 6:23); “Is thine eye evil, because I am good?” (Matthew 20:15).
The eye-lamp burns on what it gives: the palm spread to the poor is the shining.

Revelation then describes the Son three times over, and the description is the court's own:

His head and his hairs were white like wool, as white as snow; and his eyes were as a flame of fire.

The white Head of Daniel's vision — and eyes of burning flame (so again at 2:18 and 19:12, under “many crowns”).
Now we know who His eyes are: the burning ones, His righteous, sent “to and fro through the whole earth.”

Now stand outside on a clear night and say what you see: figures of animals — a lion, a bull, an eagle among them — drawn in points of light, wheeling through the whole earth in their seasons.
The beasts full of eyes are the court of heaven in figures, each figure studded with its stars — the Mazzaroth brought forth “in his season” (Job 38:32).

The pattern was copied once on earth, in the seat of the wisest king:

Moreover the king made a great throne of ivory, and overlaid it with the best gold… the top of the throne was round behind… And twelve lions stood there on the one side and on the other upon the six steps: there was not the like made in any kingdom.

White, round, and twelve beasts round about it — and seated on it, the man to whom God gave wisdom “even as the sand that is on the sea shore” (1 Kings 4:29).
Not the like in any kingdom below, for its like hangs above every kingdom: Daniel's seated One, “whose garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like the pure wool” (Daniel 7:9) — the white circle enthroned among the twelve figures of the night.

The sky does not merely decorate the pattern; it testifies to the unseen original.
The Lord pitched “the true tabernacle” in heaven (Hebrews 8:2).
God named the visible firmament Heaven (Genesis 1:8).
Moses then built the earthly sanctuary “according to the pattern” shown him, as “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Exodus 25:40; Hebrews 8:5).

The visible heaven is not the heavenly court itself, any more than the earthly tabernacle was.
It is created testimony to that court: “the invisible things of him” are “clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made” (Romans 1:20).
The unseen court is reflected in the sky and reflected again in the sanctuary.
Creation declares; the sanctuary teaches; both point beyond themselves to the same original.
This is why the heavens can declare God's glory without a spoken word: “day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge” because their very structure is teaching (Psalm 19:1-4).

.One heavenly pattern — declared by creation and taught by the sanctuary

The sky is built like a dwelling, and Scripture says so plainly: He “stretcheth out the heavens like a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in” (Isaiah 40:22); “In them hath he set a tabernacle for the sun, which is as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, and rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race” (Psalm 19:4-5).
And a dwelling has doors.
Jacob woke and named what he had seen — “this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven” (Genesis 28:17); the psalmist says He “opened the doors of heaven” to rain down manna (Psalm 78:23); John's vision begins, “behold, a door was opened in heaven” (Revelation 4:1).

The lights keep their appointments through those doors.
The bridegroom-sun comes out of his chamber to run his circuit; and Ezekiel's east gate, shut the six working days, opens on the appointed days (Ezekiel 46:1).

The city whose builder is God hangs the count on its wall: “twelve gates… and names written thereon, which are the names of the twelve tribes” (Revelation 21:12).
Twelve tribes, twelve figures of the Mazzaroth, twelve gates in the sky's house: the doors of the tabernacle above, through which the sun runs his year and the moon enters at her fulness.

Scripture ties the gates to the tribes by name, at both ends of the canon.
In the wilderness the twelve camped around the tabernacle in four triads — “on the east side toward the rising of the sun… the standard of the camp of Judah” (Numbers 2:3), Reuben's standard on the south, Ephraim's on the west, Dan's on the north.
When Ezekiel surveys the city, the camp has become architecture — “and the gates of the city shall be after the names of the tribes of Israel” (Ezekiel 48:31), three to a side — and John sees the same wall: “On the east three gates; on the north three gates; on the south three gates; and on the west three gates” (Revelation 21:13).

The earthly camp was never the original, for the sanctuary is “a copy and shadow of what is in heaven,” built “according to the pattern” shown on the mountain (Hebrews 8:5) — and the pattern stands overhead every night: twelve figures around the dwelling of God, three to a season.
Josephus and Philo both read the high priest's twelve stones, “divided into four rows of three,” as the circle the Greeks call the zodiac — “four parts, each consisting of three” — the first-century mind saw the camp in the sky without strain. [Footnote: Josephus, Antiquities 3.7.7; Philo, Life of Moses II.124. The tribe-by-tribe case — Genesis 49 and Deuteronomy 33 read against the twelve figures, with the year's head at Virgo — is set out in Time Tested Tradition.]

The standard-bearers lead their sides — Judah's lion at the sunrise gate — and the tie itself is Scripture's own: the tribes camp in triads around the dwelling, the city's gates carry their names three to a side.

Not every light keeps its station in a figure: among the twelve wander the planets.
One verse seems to curse the wanderers, so set its two witnesses side by side.
The Greek text of Jude, describing the false teachers of his letter, reads:

Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.

The Hebrew text of Jude describes the same men — with no star in the sentence:

And like waves of the sea that cast out mire and mud.

The Hebrew is Isaiah word for word — “the wicked are like the troubled sea… whose waters cast up mire and dirt” (Isaiah 57:20) — and the Greek's added figure does not change the subject: in both witnesses the curse falls on men, wicked men who keep no station, not on any light of the sky.

The Greek needs no correction either, for Jude names his source in his next breath — “Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these” (Jude 14) — and Enoch's vision says exactly which stars have the darkness reserved:

This place is the end of heaven and earth: this has become a prison for the stars and the host of heaven.
And the stars which roll over the fire are they which have transgressed the commandment of the Lord in the beginning of their rising, because they did not come forth at their appointed times.
And He was wroth with them, and bound them…

The star bound over to darkness is not the wanderer that keeps its circuit; it is the star that broke its appointed times — the lawless light, and the men who shine like it.
Read with the source Jude himself quotes, the two witnesses agree: the Hebrew condemns the wicked in Isaiah's storm-waves, the Greek condemns the same men in Enoch's time-breaking stars — and the charge inside the star-figure is precisely this book's charge, the abandoning of the appointed times.
No planet is condemned for lawful wandering — the wanderers keep their circuits and their seasons — and two of them carry the two claims this chapter has been weighing.

The king of the wanderers — the greatest of them — the Hebrews name Tzedeq: Righteousness.
And King of Righteousness is a title with an Owner: Malki-Tzedek, “first being by interpretation King of righteousness” (Hebrews 7:2) — the priest-king whose order the Messiah holds forever: “Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4).

Look at it through any glass: it wears stripes across its whole face; it bears one great wound in its side; and its color is the red-orange of a sardius stone.
John saw that stone on the throne — “he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone” (Revelation 4:3) — and Isaiah saw the marks on the Servant: “he was wounded for our transgressions… and with his stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).
The king planet wears the King's own marks — striped, pierced, sardius-red — and its Hebrew name is Righteousness.

One wanderer the nations served, and Scripture names the service:

But ye have borne the tabernacle of your Moloch and Chiun your images, the star of your god, which ye made to yourselves.

Chiun is the old name of Saturn — Stephen, quoting the verse, reads it “the star of your god Remphan” (Acts 7:43) — and Amos sets the star beside Moloch, the idol fed with children, exactly as the nations’ own stories tell of Saturn devouring his sons.
The goat-shaped devils Israel was forbidden to serve — “they shall no more offer their sacrifices unto devils” (Leviticus 17:7) — are the se'irim, the same word the King James elsewhere renders satyrs (Isaiah 13:21).

The satyr's planet comes dressed for the part: a six-sided crown of storm stands on its pole, and round about it hangs a great ring — a millstone.
“It were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and he cast into the sea, than that he should offend one of these little ones” (Luke 17:2) — the sentence pronounced on those who offend the little ones, worn as a collar by the star of the god who ate his own.
Two wanderers among the twelve: the King's, wearing the wounds and the stripes of Righteousness; and the counterfeit's, wearing the millstone.

In the next chapter we will discover how God documented Satan's plan to corrupt these signs — to change the times and the laws.
